# Temple AI Campus — Texas development dossier

**Concept / pre-feasibility proposal · 13 October 2026 · native USD · 100 MW IT in four 25 MW phases**

This is an independently scoped facility-development project. It is not a Texas benchmark for another project. The deliverable is a candidate-site investigation, technical concept, auditable economic case and executable sequence of diligence gates. It does not constitute land control, utility approval, a permit, a construction design or an investment commitment.

## Investment decision

**Advance a capped diligence program; do not authorize construction or promise an energization date.** Base-case equity returns also miss the proposed investment hurdle, so regulatory reopening alone would not justify FID. The North Temple industrial area is worth investigating for a water-conserving, liquid-cooled wholesale AI campus. A defensible commitment requires a real parcel, 140 MW peak power pathway, regulatory reopening, demonstrated thermal performance and a credit-supported anchor lease.

The controlling current fact is the Texas approval hold. The Governor's September 21 directive and TCEQ's current construction-stormwater notice prevent treating ordinary permitting times as a live schedule. TCEQ explicitly includes construction general-permit applications for data-center projects. The proposed calendar therefore contains an unknown period before **M0**, followed by a conditional 48-month first-phase path. October 19 is a requested government compliance update, not a promised reopening. [TX05](https://gov.texas.gov/news/post/governor-abbott-directs-tceq-to-halt-data-center-permits) [TX06](https://www.tceq.texas.gov/permitting/stormwater/construction/)

The asset earns capacity rent and recovers metered electricity costs. It does not purchase GPUs or sell inference/training tokens. No income is assumed from energy arbitrage, generator dispatch, tax incentives or speculative land appreciation.

## Candidate site and alternatives

The preferred investigation area is the **historically advertised 147 acres at the southwest corner of Moores Mill Road and Wendland Road, North Temple, Bell County**. Temple EDC's 2020 announcement identifies the address and road/water/sewer/rail context. This evidence establishes a real location to investigate; it does not establish that the land remains available. The conceptual gross study envelope is 59.5 hectares. [TX01](https://templeedc.com/temple-unveils-new-shovel-ready-site-in-industrial-park/)

The map marker at **31.1555256, −97.3408890** is a geographic reference on Moores Mill Road from OpenStreetMap/Nominatim. It is deliberately not presented as the tract centroid, surveyed corner or legal parcel. A diagrammed rectangular campus is an area fit study, not a survey overlay. Resolve parcel ID, owner, actual corners, setbacks, easements and developable ground before claiming this layout fits the site. [TX16](https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/1548733235)

Temple EDC currently publishes an industrial site-search service and identifies the regional utility context. Oncor is only a provisional power counterparty until the exact parcel's DSP/TSP confirms jurisdiction. Area telecom availability is not proof of diverse fiber. [TX02](https://templeedc.com/tools-resources/site-selection/) [TX03](https://templeedc.com/doing-business-here/infrastructure/)

| Candidate | Evidence | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| North Temple / Moores Mill–Wendland | Historic specific 147-acre EDC announcement; industrial access context | Preferred investigation area, subject to availability and power; no proven advantage in connection date |
| Five Points Business Park, Abilene | DCOA advertises over 500 acres of sites and a 50 MW substation | Retain alternate; stated substation size is below the campus's 140 MW requirement and is not evidence of spare capacity |
| Texas Central Park, Waco | City lists industrial development land at I-35/SH6/US84 | Retain alternate; identify a real tract and utility route before scoring its power advantage |

Abilene and Waco remain subject to the same statewide hold. Do not give artificial numerical rankings to unverified power schedules. If either alternative supplies a better verified connection and viable parcel, replace the North Temple selection. [TX12](https://developabilene.com/five-points-business-park/) [TX13](https://www.waco-texas.com/Departments/Economic-Development/Site-Selection)

Parcel diligence must cover title and option terms, ALTA/NSPS survey, Phase I environmental assessment, geotechnical borings, flood and drainage modeling, wetland screening, utility and rail easements, heavy-haul access, airport/FAA constraints, neighboring residences and acoustic setbacks. No result for these items has been established.

## Product and technical basis

Deliver four independently commissioned 25 MW IT blocks. The design target is concurrent maintenance of critical distribution and cooling, subject to a failure-mode study; no certification or availability percentage is claimed. Customer equipment and upstream network fabrics lie outside the landlord's capital boundary. A customer interface schedule must fix rack density, power quality, liquid temperatures/chemistry, maximum step load, rack weights, white-space scope and commissioning loads.

Capacity definitions must remain distinct:

- 100 MW IT is the campus's contracted design boundary.
- Annual PUE 1.28 is a planning estimate for energy accounting.
- Peak PUE 1.40 implies a preliminary **140 MW facility demand** at full IT design load.
- 90% committed occupancy is commercial utilization of built IT capacity.
- 85% IT load factor is average metered draw on that committed capacity.

At stabilized base assumptions, average IT draw is 76.5 MW and average facility draw is 97.92 MW. Annual purchased electricity is approximately **857,779 MWh** before further refinements to seasonal and fixed-load modeling. At USD80/MWh it costs approximately **USD68.62 million/year**, recovered as a separate electricity pass-through. It is not landlord operating profit. An actual tariff with demand charges needs an interval-load model; an all-in MWh allowance is an underwriting simplification.

The detailed electrical and thermal quantities belong to the shared engineering worksheet and accompanying concept drawings. They must be reconciled before procurement. The electrical concept uses a provisional 138 kV intake, an N+1 transformer capacity arrangement, sectional medium-voltage distribution, block UPS and emergency standby sized for design cooling auxiliaries as well as IT. Final voltage, fault duty, protection settings and grounding depend on the utility study. Dual switchboards do not establish independent utility supply.

A minimum 100 MW energy balance flows through the tenant equipment. At the assumed 90% direct-liquid capture, 90 MW goes to the liquid circuit and 10 MW remains for room-air cooling, before pumping, UPS and refrigeration heat. At a 10 K liquid temperature difference, 90 MW corresponds to roughly 2,150 kg/s water-equivalent circulation. This is **recirculated heat-transfer flow**, not daily water consumption.

### Power pathway

Submit one disclosed full-campus demand/ramp. A four-phase build does not create four independent exemptions from large-load rules. The project's expected facility demand exceeds ERCOT's 75 MW large-load threshold. It has no existing queue position or demonstrated Batch Zero eligibility; the published July 2026 intake dates have passed. The first task is obtaining the applicable post-hold entry route from the interconnecting utility/ERCOT, not assuming historic serial-queue treatment. [TX04](https://www.ercot.com/services/rq/large-load-integration/)

The adopted **16 TAC §25.194, effective October 8, 2026**, requires material commercial/technical disclosures and financial commitments. At 140 MW requested peak, the stated USD50,000/MW intermediate security basis yields **USD7 million**, with a **USD100,000 study fee**. Final security can be higher because it is tied to the greater of the prescribed per-MW amount and allocated upgrade costs. Confirm all tariff, credit, milestone and return/forfeiture terms with counsel and the utility. Security is separately modeled liquidity, not a second copy of construction cost. [TX07, printed pages 6931–6940](https://www.sos.state.tx.us/texreg/pdf/backview/1002/1002is.pdf)

Required studies include steady-state and contingency power flow, short circuit, protection coordination, dynamic behavior/ride-through, harmonics and any subsynchronous issues. Model UPS and chiller response, IT load steps, fault recovery and restoration—not simply a flat MW number. Commission agreed telemetry, metering and protection and obtain explicit authorization before each energization stage.

Choose grid supply with emergency generators in the base case. A prime-power gas alternative is a separate project requiring firm gas supply and pressure, emissions/air authorization, operability and maintenance reserves, noise controls and finance. It is not a presumed route around the state data-center permit hold. Emergency equipment must not be underwritten for routine economic dispatch without explicit environmental and contractual permission.

### Cooling, weather and water

Use direct-to-chip CDUs and segregated secondary circuits, dry heat rejection and air-cooled mechanical trim, with independently maintainable pump and heat-rejection modules. Mechanical trim is essential when outdoor temperature exceeds the useful dry-cooler approach to the customer loop. An annual average temperature cannot size this system.

Use 43°C dry bulb as a provisional engineering screen and 46°C as a stress case, subject to local design-weather review and vendor curves. NWS's Waco record is a regional proxy showing both hot summers and freezes; it is not the Temple design weather file. Include hail/wind damage resistance, freeze protection, heat-trace needs and loss-of-cooling recovery. Validate annual PUE using an hourly simulation at customer-required liquid temperatures. [TX09](https://www.weather.gov/fwd/act_normals)

The base design has no evaporative cooling towers. Its initial domestic/service allowance is **15 m³/day**, approximately 5,475 m³/year, excluding separately estimated first fill and emergency fire events. It is not a municipal allocation. At the modeled full-campus average IT energy, that allowance would be roughly 0.008 L/kWh; this arithmetic is a scope-limited domestic-water indicator, not a measured campus WUE. Count all actual water sources, fill, makeup, discharge and construction use before making any efficiency claim. Obtain City service, fire-flow and drought terms; no groundwater wells or new water rights are assumed. TWDB's operational survey obligations are distinct from water service authorization. [TX08](https://www.twdb.texas.gov/waterplanning/waterusesurvey/digitalinfrastructure.asp)

Two physically independent fiber paths require traced carrier routes, separate site entrances, separated duct banks and restoration commitments. Two invoices or two carrier logos do not prove diversity. No route or latency claim is presently supported.

## Permissions and implementation sequence

The permit matrix in `project.json` covers state reopening, local land/building permissions, large-load studies, air authorization, construction stormwater, municipal water/fire and conditional environmental constraints. All are unfulfilled for this proposal.

The City department is the starting point for actual parcel jurisdiction, use classification, plat/site-plan, building/MEP and certificate-of-occupancy requirements. Its exact data-center treatment and adopted code editions need confirmation. Plan drainage and access with the same surveyed site; do not assume industrial marketing establishes permitted use. [TX11](https://www.templetx.gov/departments/city_departments/building_permits___inspections/index.php)

An air specialist must assess the entire standby fleet and fuel storage together, with engine run hours, test concurrency, emissions factors and dispersion. Determine the required NSR/PBR/Title V route and federal engine requirements. This concept does not certify eligibility for a permit by rule. [TX10](https://www.tceq.texas.gov/permitting/air/air_permits.html)

Construction stormwater coverage and SWP3 must precede relevant earthworks. The statewide hold currently affects this route; a municipal building permit would not replace it. Renewals and rule changes must be checked at the actual start, since the assumed development schedule extends beyond current permit dates. [TX06](https://www.tceq.texas.gov/permitting/stormwater/construction/)

Procurement is conditional on adequate design certainty. The base first-operation assumption is now **M48**, providing 30 months from the M12 HV release to M42 delivery, four months for installation/SAT and two for integrated acceptance. M42 operation is not credible on this ordering sequence. Early transformer releases at M12 create at-risk deposits and cancellation liabilities before the M18 FID and require separate sponsor approval. If preliminary utility data cannot freeze the interface by M12, move the release and downstream dates; do not shorten the lead time without supplier evidence. ## Procurement and acceptance package

No supplier has quoted these quantities or dates. Planning lead allowances are 30 months for the HV package, 24 for MV switchgear/protection, 22 for UPS/standby, 18 for liquid/trim cooling, 16 for shell/civil and 12 for fiber/controls. Obtain at least two credible bids for critical equipment, define freight/tax/escalation, cancellation exposure, factory slots, spare strategy and performance warranties. Lead-time figures in this proposal are estimates.

Each request for quotation must include peak and continuous duty, Texas summer derating, fault ratings, load-step requirements, shipping dimensions, remote-monitoring/OT security, maintenance access, test procedures and clear battery limits. Owner-furnished equipment interfaces must be assigned in the EPC contract.

Commissioning progresses through design review, factory tests, receipt checks, pre-functional testing, system functional testing and integrated failure/load testing. Prove loss of utility, failed generator/UPS module, failed cooling module, sensor faults, controls communication loss, water leakage and recovery from curtailment with simulated tenant load. Verify peak thermal performance, power metering, protection/telemetry and fiber diversity. Tenant acceptance, approved operating procedures and complete as-builts—not merely mechanical completion—start rent.

## Commercial and financial underwriting

Offer 15-year wholesale capacity leases with electricity billed separately on a defined metering/PUE basis. Target a creditworthy 50 MW anchor, then a second customer or anchor expansion for the remaining phases. No counterparties have been contacted and no demand is represented as secured.

The model horizon is 20 years from the first COD, but the proposed initial lease term is 15 years per phase. It therefore includes **60, 54, 48 and 42 months of uncontracted renewal/reletting revenue** for phases 1–4. That tail assumes unchanged rent and occupancy, no downtime and no renewal CAPEX. It is an explicit underwriting assumption, not part of the initial take-or-pay lease. A lender case must haircut or remove the tail and fund reletting costs; no present customer contract supports it.

Specify liquid temperature/chemistry and density limits, capacity ramp, acceptance conditions, utility delay relief, customer fit-out boundary, rent commencement, delivery long-stop date, curtailment terms and SLA remedies. Use a parent guarantee or acceptable bank security. A flexible training workload and a strict always-on inference SLA are different products; price them accordingly.

| Base planning input | Value and basis |
|---|---|
| Facility hard cost | USD10,000/kW IT; USD1.0bn at 100 MW. Shell 1,800; electrical/UPS/standby 4,000; cooling 2,200; civil/drainage 1,000; controls/security/fiber 500; testing/commissioning 500 per kW |
| Land | USD12m allowance; not an owner asking price |
| HV connection/upgrades | USD65m off-plot utility allowance; customer-owned HV substation is in facility electrical; not a study outcome |
| Primary power plant | Zero; emergency standby included in facility cost |
| Soft costs / contingency | 10% / 15% on bases documented in the shared model |
| Utility security | USD7m separate liquidity reserve; actual amount and release timing unconfirmed |
| Fixed facility OPEX | USD30m/year at stabilization: property-tax 18m, insurance 4m, staff/security 6m, administration/compliance 2m |
| Variable facility OPEX | USD55/kW/year on the shared model's defined capacity basis |
| Electricity | USD80/MWh delivered placeholder; test USD55–125/MWh |
| Capacity rent | USD195/kW/month; test USD150–250; no signed price evidence |
| Occupancy / IT load factor | 90% / 85%, treated separately |
| Debt | 60%, 8% interest, 15-year amortization; no lender offer |
| Equity screening rate | 14% nominal; no investor commitment |

With the current shared model, base CAPEX is **USD1,362.4m** before interest and collateral, and total modeled funding is approximately **USD1,456.4m** including capitalized interest and the USD7m reserve. Stabilized capacity rent is **USD210.6m/year**, EBITDA **USD175.65m/year**, and cash flow before debt service after the maintenance reserve **USD165.65m/year**. Minimum annual operating DSCR is approximately **1.60**, but equity IRR is only **10.2%**, below the 14% hurdle, and equity NPV is approximately **−USD94.9m**. The model requires approximately **USD218/kW/month** capacity rent to achieve a 14% equity NPV break-even with other assumptions unchanged. This is an estimated required rent, not a market quote. The investment recommendation therefore remains **no FID at base inputs**. Recalculate these outputs after any change.

The financial model currently spreads common land and off-plot utility capital over M1–12, before the proposed M18 FID. This is a conservative early-cash-exposure assumption, not an authorization to spend or a representation of the gated execution plan. Rephase those cash flows to actual option, utility-deposit and construction milestones before financing; the model does not yet separately price pre-FID cancellation losses.

All values are illustrative estimates in USD. The shared calculation workbook/module is authoritative for totals, phasing, debt, DSCR, unlevered/levered cash flow and sensitivity; this narrative does not substitute a separate spreadsheet formula chain. Its documented limitations, including income tax, inflation, terminal value and reserve treatment, apply.

The landed facility unit budget includes a general procurement-tax allowance, without crediting a data-center exemption. Texas publishes eligibility rules for state sales-tax relief, but no award or continuing entitlement is assumed here. Verify property-tax districts and assessed value independently; an electricity exemption is not a property-tax exemption. [TX14](https://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/data-centers/)

Use a downside combining facility CAPEX +25%, utility upgrades +USD50m, rent −15%, occupancy 75%, PUE 1.40 and a 12-month post-restart delay. Electricity largely passes through economically, but higher bills affect competitiveness, credit exposure and tenant willingness to commit. Do not label the project financeable solely because an optimistic base DSCR exceeds 1.30. Require lender-defined downside DSCR, a sponsor-approved equity hurdle and enough equity for taxes, working capital, utility collateral and uninsured delay.

## Risks, gates and immediate diligence

The most material risks are the state hold, unknown power allocation/upgrades, a historic tract that may be unavailable, anchor credit/ramp, hot-weather performance, unconfirmed water/fire/fiber, generator authorization and equipment delivery. The machine-readable risk register assigns impacts, mitigation, triggers and accountable roles. None is eliminated by a polished model.

Gate order is: **G0 lawful restart → G1 site control → G2 power/water → G3 bankable demand → G4 FID → G5 staged energization → G6 accepted tenant handover.** Some evidence gathering runs in parallel, but capital release follows the relevant gates. An existing utility queue elsewhere or industrial site's advertised substation does not prove this project has secured capacity. [TX15](https://www.oncor.com/content/oncorwww/wire/en/home/newsroom/oncor-reports-first-quarter-2026-results.html)

For the next four weeks, prepare the following requests without implying they have been sent:

1. **Regulatory counsel:** current hold interpretation, lawful diligence boundary, post-hold large-load path and collateral obligations. Stop if the proposed route relies on an unconfirmed exemption.
2. **EDC/landowner:** parcel IDs, current availability, owner authority, survey, restrictions and conditional option terms. Replace the tract if it is unavailable or fails physical fit.
3. **DSP/TSP:** 140 MW peak request, four-stage IT ramp, product/UPS/generator profile, candidate POIs and study/security process. Require actual project evidence before a delivery promise.
4. **Civil/City:** flood, wetland, geotechnical and airport screening, land-use classification, municipal service/fire-flow and drought terms.
5. **OEMs/carriers/tenants:** comparable budget quotations, thermal curves, physical fiber routes and credit-supported customer requirements.

A sponsor could authorize an initial **USD250,000 desktop diligence cap** as an estimate, with separate approval for surveys/fieldwork and no nonrefundable land purchase or equipment order until the corresponding gate. A complete utility study and full pre-FID development effort require a much larger, separately approved budget plus security. These are proposed spending gates; no money has been committed.

Kill or replace the project if the land cannot be controlled; 140 MW cannot be connected on viable terms; the current approval pathway has no acceptable resolution at the sponsor's six-month review; a 50 MW creditworthy anchor cannot be contracted; or combined downside fails finance and return hurdles. Maintain the full 100 MW concept while releasing each next phase only against evidence.

# Texas execution package

**Temple AI Campus · 100 MW IT · 13 October 2026 · concept / pre-feasibility · USD**

This appendix turns the proposal into work packages, proposed contract terms and acceptance evidence. Every date, staffing figure and target below is a planning assumption. It is not an approved operating procedure or purchase authorization. All request templates are **unsent**.

## Delivery logic and capital releases

M0 is a future authorized restart after regulatory clearance. The current hold adds an unknown period before this clock. Base first acceptance is **M48**, with cumulative 50/75/100 MW IT at M54/M60/M66.

The 30-month HV allowance is measured from a technically frozen order to arrival on site, including factory tests and freight. The sequence is M12 order → M42 delivery → M46 installation/site tests → M48 integrated acceptance. An order first released at M18 FID instead yields a minimum M54 first COD on the same allowances. Utility or permit delay moves the entire path.

An M12 purchase creates real pre-FID cancellation exposure. Authorize it separately only after the utility interface is mature, the land option permits the intended development, supplier terms identify the exposure and equity can absorb a cancellation. A refundable slot reservation is not treated as a full equipment order unless the supplier commits the manufacturing start and delivery date. The shared financial model uses a simplified early common-cost cash curve; replace it with accepted contract milestones before financial close.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSP interface and off-site works | M0–12; settle voltage, peak/ramp, fault levels and protection boundary | Study/connection scope by M18; field completion target M42–46 | Energization authority before M46–48 tests | Power lead; utility agreement and funded security |
| Four 50 MVA primary transformers and associated HV equipment | RFQ M3–9; technical freeze M12 | M12 release; 30 months to M42 on-site | M42–46 SAT; no capacity accepted before tests | EPC electrical lead; separately approved pre-FID exposure |
| First-block MV/LV package | RFQ M9–12; interface freeze M16 | M16 release; 24 months to M40 | M40–46, coordinated with protection tests | Electrical lead; conditional release then FID |
| First-block UPS / emergency standby | RFQ M12–16; duty and net ratings frozen M18 | M18 release; 22 months to M40 | M40–46 SAT; M46–48 integrated test | Electrical/air leads; compliant engine specification and permitted operating envelope |
| First-block CDUs / dry rejection / trim | RFQ M14–18; customer temperatures frozen M20 | M20 release; 18 months to M38 | M38–44 assembly; M44–48 thermal/controls tests | MEP lead; customer interface, water and structural design |
| Civil / first hall | Survey/design M0–18 | Permitted enabling works M18–28; hall package M24 onward | Weather-tight target M36; ready for MEP and commissioning | Civil/EPC lead; permits, FID, drainage and access |

## Commissioning and acceptance matrix

The owner’s engineer and tenant must approve the final test specification before equipment release. Proposed numeric targets below define what a tender must answer; they are not manufacturer guarantees. Tests use approved switching, safety and load-bank plans under competent site supervision.

| System / test | Proposed measurable acceptance evidence | Required input still unresolved | Witness / release |
|---|---|---|---|
| IT capacity and metering | Demonstrate 25 MW IT continuously for an initial 8-hour capacity run per block; calibrated IT and facility meters reconcile within an agreed 1% accounting tolerance | Actual tenant load-bank profile, instrument accuracy, allowable transient envelope | Independent commissioning authority + tenant; rent start only after accepted report |
| Peak thermal duty | Equipment schedule supports 35 MW facility heat rejection per block at 43°C dry bulb with one 5 MW rejection module unavailable; document 46°C stress-case output and any derating | Site design weather, vendor curves, exact indoor conditions, glycol properties, fan/pump power | MEP engineer; OEM certified curves plus witnessed functional evidence; annual PUE remains modeled until measured |
| CDU/liquid path | 22.5 MW liquid duty per block at the agreed 35/45°C facility-loop basis, with one 2.5 MW CDU unavailable; balance and record flows, pressures and temperatures | Tenant secondary-loop temperature/chemistry, HX approach, pipe losses and allowed pressure | MEP + customer engineer; no final guarantee until interface is agreed |
| Residual room cooling | Demonstrate 2.5 MW residual IT heat per block plus relevant room losses, within tenant rack inlet limits, under one specified component fault | Exact air-cooled equipment share, air-flow paths and inlet limits | MEP/tenant; independent room cooling path required |
| Primary transformer resilience | At 140 MW campus peak and PF ≥0.95, 3 remaining 50 MVA units retain ≥147.37 MVA aggregate capacity; document that buses and protection can actually deliver it | TSP fault levels, impedance, sectionalization and common-mode studies | Electrical engineer + utility; arithmetic alone cannot release the gate |
| UPS N+1 and battery | Each block sustains 25 MW IT with one 5 MW module unavailable; demonstrate the specified 5-minute delivered autonomy or an accepted equivalent test | End-of-life battery sizing, temperature/discharge margin, actual voltage/frequency limits | OEM + commissioning authority; no interruption outside the approved customer envelope |
| Utility failure / standby | Each block has 35 MW net standby duty after one unit unavailable; integrated utility-loss and restoration tests stay inside customer electrical and thermal envelopes | Site-derated 5 MW unit ratings, start/load-step time, transfer/protection sequence and cooling/control ride-through | Utility, OEM, commissioning authority and tenant; UPS-only IT support does not prove cooling continuity |
| Fuel resilience | Verify tank usable volume against an initial **24-hour design-runtime target** at agreed critical load; independently test telemetry, containment and delivery access | OEM fuel curve, legally permitted storage, replenishment SLA and outage demand; runtime is not yet proven | Environmental/fire/operations leads; revise target or CAPEX before contract if infeasible |
| Fault / maintenance isolation | Complete a failure-mode matrix covering each electrical/cooling isolation boundary; witness representative failures with no loss outside the contractual tolerance | Agreed single-failure set, allowed maintenance windows and tenant tolerance | Independent commissioning authority; no certified availability claim |
| Fiber diversity | As-built route audit confirms two separate paths and entrances; demonstrate agreed service continuity under one carrier/path failure | Latency, bandwidth, packet loss/recovery limits and verified off-site shared structures | Network engineer + tenant; two carriers alone do not pass |
| Water / leak response | Verify separate mains/makeup metering, measured service pressure/flow and leak alarm/valve response to an approved test; record commissioning fill separately | City allocation, fire-flow design, domestic actuals and leakage response time | Civil/MEP/fire authorities; 15 m³/day is an allowance, not a pass/fail demand guarantee |
| Controls / cyber / handover | All critical points commissioned; all critical alarms delivered and acknowledged; restore from tested configuration backup; zero open critical defects at acceptance | Asset inventory, OT threat assessment, alarm classification and tenant interfaces | Controls lead + owner; signed as-builts, training, spares and operating procedures required |

The integrated proving period is an initial **72-hour owner target** under agreed varying load and approved fault demonstrations. Eight-hour individual capacity runs may form part of it. Do not promise a 43°C ambient site test on a particular date: use certified performance mapping plus witnessed testing, or defer seasonal verification with an agreed retention and remedy. No unavailable criterion may be silently treated as passed.

## Operating organization and budget basis

At full build, assume **40 direct operations FTE** as a scoping allowance: 24 rotating critical-facility FTE covering four simultaneous posts, with six FTE per post for roster/leave/training relief, 8 day-maintenance/controls positions, 4 facility management/compliance/planning positions and 4 network/service coordination positions. This is not a staffing minimum derived from law or an OEM requirement. Validate skill mix, shift calendars, absence/training relief and local labor costs before contracting. Physical security is a separately contracted 24/7 service, included in the staff/security budget allowance rather than these 40 FTE.

The existing USD6m/year staffing/security provision can provisionally allocate USD4.8m to 40 direct FTE at USD120,000 loaded annual cost each and USD1.2m to contracted security. Both are owner estimates, not market salary or vendor quotes. They may be inadequate once overtime, benefits and the actual security-post plan are priced; replace them before FID. OEM emergency support and specialized maintenance also draw on variable OPEX and the maintenance reserve. Texas's fixed OPEX includes separate property-tax, insurance and compliance/admin allowances.

| Responsibility | Staffing / service assumption | Routine control | Escalation and evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Incident command and dispatch | One appointed shift lead; continuous critical facilities coverage | Shift handover, alarm review, permit-to-work, change freeze during incidents | Immediate critical alarm response, owner incident commander and tenant notice under agreed SLA; timed event log |
| Electrical distribution, UPS and standby | Electrical specialists plus contracted OEM support | OEM- and risk-based PM, battery trends, protection maintenance, thermography under approved procedures | Duty capacity loss or unresolved protection defect stops affected maintenance/acceptance; incident and repair record |
| Cooling and water | Mechanical technicians and OEM specialist availability | Temperature/pressure/flow trends, leak checks, water chemistry, heat-exchanger cleanliness, freeze/hail readiness | Projected temperature breach triggers approved load-management escalation; environmental release follows response plan |
| Network and controls | Service coordination plus managed network/OT service | Route health, authenticated changes, configuration backup/restore, access reviews | Carrier failure to diverse path; OT incident isolates per approved plan and alerts security/tenant |
| Safety, environment and permits | Accountable compliance lead and specialist contractors | Permit conditions register, generator run-hour/fuel records, water reports, SWP3 during works, tank/fire inspections | Any permit limit breach escalates immediately to management; legal notification deadlines recorded by counsel |
| Commercial / asset management | Facility manager + off-site commercial/finance support | Meter-based invoices, SLA calculation, rent/credit monitoring, insurance and tax calendar | Credit-support shortfall, claims or DSCR covenant trigger to CFO and lender under agreed documents |

Before each phase opens, build a computerized maintenance system containing OEM intervals, criticality, work methods, trained personnel and spare links. No generic interval in this appendix overrides the approved OEM/permit requirement. Initial on-site spares should cover sensors, control modules, approved fuses/breakers, pump seals/motors, valves/actuators, compatible UPS modules and critical fan drives. Transformer and generator major spares need a priced pooled or OEM support arrangement; they are not assumed on a shelf.

Maintain tested emergency procedures for utility loss, failed generator, cooling interruption, leak, fire, severe weather, fuel disruption, security/OT incident and evacuation. Rehearse non-disruptive scenarios quarterly as an owner planning target and revalidate after topology changes; disruptive exercises require approved windows. Annual management review reconciles actual water/energy/PUE, engine hours/emissions, PM backlog, insurance, asset condition and maintenance capital.

The compliance register must identify each permit or agreement, responsible person, record retention, reporting period, legal deadline, evidence file and escalation contact. TCEQ engine limits, TWDB reporting, City water/fire conditions, utility/ERCOT metering/protection and local occupancy requirements are project-specific. No permit numbers or reporting dates are fabricated here.

## Proposed anchor lease heads of terms

These are discussion positions, not an offer, signed contract or legal opinion. Counsel and lenders must settle enforceable terms.

| Topic | Proposed position / unresolved commercial choice |
|---|---|
| Premises and capacity | Dedicated suites totaling a 50 MW anchor across two accepted 25 MW blocks; remaining capacity subject to paid, milestone-limited options |
| Initial term | 15 years separately from acceptance of each block; renewal rights and pricing negotiated separately |
| Base rent | USD195 per committed IT kW/month starting after objective acceptance; illustrative price, not a quote |
| Electricity | Separately metered cost pass-through with documented PUE/allocation method, losses, taxes, demand charges, curtailment treatment and audit rights; no landlord energy margin assumed |
| Credit | Parent guarantee or acceptable bank LC sized by independent credit review; replenish on use/downgrade; no unsecured AI venture assumption |
| Tenant boundary | Tenant owns IT/network assets and provides density, inlet/liquid-temperature, heat split, loading and load-step requirements before design freeze |
| Availability | Define electrical/thermal service envelope, maintenance windows and agreed curtailment; credits and caps priced after failure-mode analysis; no unproven Tier/uptime promise |
| Delivery and conditions | Conditional dates tied to regulatory restart, permits, utility ramp and customer design; long-stop, termination costs and extension rights explicitly negotiated |
| Capacity ramp | Binding take-or-pay ramp after accepted delivery; tenant-caused delay/late fit-out treatment and landlord commissioning access defined |
| Construction changes | Written change control allocates customer redesign, scope changes, fuel/air requirements and added redundancy to cost and schedule |
| Insurance / liability | Agree insured risks, deductibles, casualty/restoration, consequential-damage treatment, limitation caps, force majeure and lender step-in |
| End of term | Reinstatement, tenant equipment removal, environmental responsibilities, renewal notice and residual works; no automatic renewal revenue represented |

The model assumes later phases reach 90% occupancy immediately and continues rent after each initial lease. The resulting uncontracted tail is 60/54/48/42 months across phases 1–4. Underwriting must explicitly evaluate renewal downtime, new fit-out costs and rent reset; the current model does not price those items.

> Carrier: supply two end-to-end route drawings, shared structures, entrance and diversity evidence, bandwidth/latency SLA, build costs and restoration terms. City: confirm parcel use, approvals, water/fire capacity and drought/discharge conditions against an initial 15 m³/day domestic/service allowance and separately designed fill/fire needs. Prospective anchor: provide credit support, capacity/ramp, thermal and power-quality requirements, curtailment tolerance and pricing response to the proposed rent plus transparent electricity pass-through. No interest or service availability will be represented without written evidence.

Returned evidence should be dated, attributed, scoped and retained in the project data room. Change the assumption register and model only after reconciling the reply's limits and interfaces. Escalate contradictory responses before releasing the next capital gate.

## Model qualifications

- Concept estimates, not contractor quotes, grid rights, permit approvals or a financing offer.
- Pre-tax, constant nominal inputs: no inflation/escalation, corporate/income tax, depreciation, grants, terminal asset value or GPU purchases.
- PUE is an annual input, not an hourly weather simulation; low-load fixed power and demand ratchets are not modeled.
- Electricity is passed through at cost; changes affect tenant cost, not landlord EBITDA. Owned-plant energy price must contain variable generation costs only.
- No lease ramp: each commissioned phase immediately reaches the chosen occupancy. Schedule is conditional, not a forecast of approval.
- Returns use monthly timing; annual DSCR uses cash available after maintenance capital, including any final debt balloon.
- Pre-tax, un-escalated planning model; no depreciation, income tax, incentives or GPU assets.
- No terminal sale proceeds or land salvage; utility collateral returns at the modeled horizon.
- No lease-up ramp: occupancy applies from each phase commissioning date.
- Maintenance reserve is preliminary; plant major overhauls and tenant equipment levy require separate diligence.
